title: Data Validation and Domain Constraints
learningObjectives: Explain validation as checking whether data satisfies expected rules.
Distinguish type validity from domain or business-rule validity.
Identify required, range, format, and cross-field constraints.
Recognize why client-side validation must not replace trusted server-side checks.
Design clear validation failures without silently changing invalid inputs.

understand.concept: Data validation checks whether input is acceptable for a particular purpose. Type or format validation asks whether a value has the expected shape, while domain constraints ask whether it is allowed in the context—for example, an order quantity must be positive and available. Constraints may apply to individual fields or relationships among multiple fields.
understand.whyItMatters: Validating at the boundaries reduces bad data, unexpected behavior, and downstream errors. It also helps preserve integrity when input comes from users, files, APIs, devices, or other systems.
understand.analogy: A ticket counter checks more than whether a ticket is printed. It may also check the date, destination, seat, and whether the ticket is valid for that journey. Data rules work similarly.
understand.analogyLimit: Validation is context-dependent and cannot prove that all data is truthful or safe. Some checks require database state, authorization, business logic, or trusted server-side processing.

explain.narrative: Define rules explicitly: required fields, length, format, numeric ranges, allowed values, relationships, and state-dependent constraints. Validate as early as practical for feedback, and validate again at trusted boundaries. Client checks improve usability but can be bypassed. Do not merely sanitize or silently normalize invalid input when the intended behavior is to reject it; return actionable errors and keep the data's meaning intact.

examples.title: Required field
examples.explanation: A name must not be blank after trimming; whether whitespace normalization is stored is a separate policy.

examples.title: Range constraint
examples.explanation: The type and permitted range are checked together for an order quantity.

examples.title: Format constraint
examples.explanation: A simple format check demonstrates a constraint but is not a complete email validation rule.

examples.title: Cross-field constraint
examples.explanation: The relationship between two fields must be valid, not merely each field individually.

examples.title: Server-side revalidation
examples.code: // Validate submitted quantity and stock on the trusted server before saving
examples.expectedOutput: Reject or accept based on server rules
examples.explanation: Client-side checks can be altered or bypassed; authoritative validation must occur at the trusted boundary.

commonMistakes: Treating a correct type as proof that a value is acceptable.
Using overly permissive format checks as complete validation.
Relying only on browser/client validation for important decisions.
Silently coercing or trimming values in ways that change their meaning.
Validating fields individually while ignoring cross-field or state-dependent constraints.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Test a data rule with examples
guidedTask.instructions: Apply "Data Validation and Domain Constraints" to a small program scenario. Work through the rule and explain the result.
steps: State what the data represents and what behavior is expected.
Identify the relevant comparison, constraint, or semantic rule.
Evaluate one valid case and one invalid or edge case.
Explain the result and any side effects.
Describe a test that would prevent a regression.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Write a small test example here

independentTask.title: Independent: Build a data-rule test
independentTask.instructions: Design and test a small scenario using this lesson's concept.
requirements: State the rule or intended behavior.
Test at least one normal case.
Test one boundary, invalid, or unusual case.
Explain how the program should respond.

hints: Describe the intended behavior before writing the condition.
Separate format/type checks from business rules.
Include a boundary or negative case in your tests.
Use exact language-specific comparison or assignment semantics.
Explain why the chosen rule is correct for this context.
